What's gone wrong?”

I says:

“Pap and mam and sis, and—”

Then I couldn't go on. He says:

“Oh, blame it, now, don't carry on like that; everybody's got their troubles, and this one'll turn out all right. What's happened to 'em?”

“They're—they're—are you the boat's watchman?”

“Yes,” he says, looking tolerable pleased with himself. “I'm captain, owner, mate, pilot, watchman, and chief deck-hand; and now and then I'm the cargo and the passengers, too. I ain't got old Jim Hornback's riches, and I can't go being so blamed generous to every Tom, Dick, and Harry, flinging money about like he does; but many's the time I've told him I wouldn't swap with him. A sailor's life is what suits me, says I, and I'll be derned if I'd settle two miles outside town, with never a thing happening, for all his cash and twice the amount besides. Says I—”

I cut in and says:

“They're in a dreadful fix, and—”

“Who are?”

“Why, pap and mam and sis and Miss Hooker; and if you'd go up there in your ferry-boat—”

“Up where? Where have they got to?”

“Out on the wreck.”

“Which wreck?”

“Why, there's only the one.”

“What! You ain't talking about the Walter Scott?”

“Yes.”

“Good gracious! What on earth are they doing there?”

“Well, it wasn't where they meant to go.”

“I should think not! Great goodness, they haven't a chance unless they get away mighty soon! How in creation did they land themselves in a mess like that?”

“Easy enough. Miss Hooker was visiting the town up there—”

“Yes, Booth's Landing. Go ahead.”

“She'd been visiting at Booth's Landing, and when evening was just coming on she took her black woman across in the horse-ferry, meaning to spend the night with a friend, Miss What's-her-name—I can't recollect it. Then they lost the steering-oar, swung round, and drifted stern foremost for about two miles, till they straddled the wreck. The ferryman and the woman and all the horses was drowned, but Miss Hooker caught hold and pulled herself aboard the wreck. Well, maybe an hour after dark, along we come in our trading-scow, and we couldn't see the wreck in the darkness till we was right against it; so we straddled it, too. Everybody got saved except Bill Whipple—and oh, there never was a kinder cretur! I pretty near wish it had been me instead, I do.”

“By George! That's the most outlandish thing I ever heard.”

Few could claim a heart so unblemished, or such true humility of spirit united with a steadfast trust in her own honour and a faith in the honour of others. She had led a secluded existence from her earliest years. Her mother had died while she was very young, but her father had given himself entirely to overseeing her education. He held many singular opinions, and these shaped the plan he followed in bringing her up. She knew well the heroes of Greece and Rome, and those English heroes who had flourished some centuries earlier, yet knew almost nothing of the events unfolding around her. Few of the authors she had read had written within the preceding fifty years, though apart from this limitation her reading was exceedingly wide. Thus, while she seemed less familiar than he with the secrets of society and life, her knowledge went deeper and rested upon sounder ground; and even had her loveliness and gentleness failed to enchant him, her mind would always have kept his captive. He regarded her as his guide, and adored her so completely that he took pleasure in heightening, in his own thoughts, the feeling of inferiority she sometimes inspired.

His mother died when he was nineteen. At this loss he departed from college, and, setting aside his former companions for a time, withdrew to the neighbourhood where his Diana lived. All his comfort came from her gentle voice and her still dearer caresses. This brief absence from his friends gave him the resolution to declare his independence. He felt that, however much they might mock his proposed marriage, they would not venture to show their scorn once it was accomplished. He therefore sought his guardian's permission, which he gained with some trouble, and that of his beloved's father, which was granted more readily. Without informing anyone else of his design, he had made Diana his wife by the time he reached his twentieth birthday.

He loved her ardently, and her tenderness exercised a charm over him that left no room for thoughts of anyone else. He asked some college friends to visit, but their shallowness revolted him. Diana had rent the veil that had hitherto confined him to boyhood: now he was a man. He wondered that he could ever have shared the stock expressions and opinions of his fellow students, or for an instant have dreaded the disapproval of such people. He relinquished those earlier friendships, not through inconstancy, but because they were truly beneath him.

You won't, will you? Oh, you prize fool!”

“It's wicked, isn't it, Oliver?” asked Charley Bates. “He'll end up getting stretched, won't he?”

“I don't know what that means,” Oliver replied.

“Something like this, old fellow,” said Charley. He seized one end of his neckerchief and held it upright in the air, then let his head fall against his shoulder and forced a strange noise through his teeth. This spirited little performance made it clear that getting stretched and getting hanged meant the same thing.

“That's what it means,” said Charley. “Look at him staring, Jack! I've never met anybody half as entertaining as this boy. He'll be the death of me, I know it.” After another hearty fit of laughter, Master Charley Bates returned to his pipe with tears in his eyes.

“You've had a bad upbringing,” said the Dodger, inspecting his boots with great satisfaction now that Oliver had polished them. “But Fagin will make something of you, or you'll be the first boy he's ever taken on who didn't pay his way. You'd better start now. You'll be in the business much sooner than you think, and you're only wasting time, Oliver.”

Master Bates supported this advice with several moral lectures of his own. Once he had finished, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins began enthusiastically describing the many pleasures of their way of life. They scattered throughout their account various hints that Oliver's wisest course would be to earn Fagin's approval immediately, using the same methods by which they had won it themselves.

“And always keep this in mind, Nolly,” said the Dodger, as they heard the Jewish man's key in the door upstairs. “If you don't lift rags and tickers—”

“What's the point of talking like that?” Master Bates interrupted. “He doesn't know what you mean.”

“If you don't steal handkerchiefs and watches,” the Dodger said, adjusting his language to Oliver's understanding, “some other fellow will. So the fellows who lose them are worse off, and you're worse off too, and nobody gains a penny except the fellows who take them. You've got just as much right to them as they have.”

“Exactly, exactly!” said the Jewish man, who had entered without Oliver noticing. “There it is in a nutshell, my dear, a nutshell. Take the Dodger's word for it. Ha, ha, ha! He knows his trade's articles of faith.”

The old man rubbed his hands together gleefully as he confirmed the Dodger's argument, chuckling with delight at his pupil's expertise.

The discussion went no further just then. The Jewish man had come home with Miss Betsy and a gentleman Oliver had never seen, whom the Dodger greeted as Tom Chitling. Having stayed behind on the stairs to exchange a few flirtatious remarks with the lady, this gentleman now appeared.
